items.excerpt: After several records examining language (Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat), mutation (Mutate), liturgical memory (Ison), and the algorithmic logic of social media (Kitbashing), Abadir arrives at what feels like the conceptual centre of his work. items.body: After several records examining language (Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat), mutation (Mutate), liturgical memory (Ison), and the algorithmic logic of social media (Kitbashing), Abadir arrives at what feels like the conceptual centre of his work. The Primitivist is not simply a new collection of club tracks but a declaration of intent, rejecting electronic music’s enduring fixation with futurism in favour of a deeper engagement with the present and with the musical traditions that continue to shape it. The title is deliberately provocative. As Abadir has argued in an article for Cartography of Darkness, electronic music has spent decades equating novelty with the future, often reproducing the same cyberpunk imagery, dystopian fantasies and technological narratives inherited from the 1980s and 1990s. For him, that obsession has become a form of nostalgia masquerading as progress, one increasingly detached from the realities of communities living through war, authoritarianism and displacement. The Primitivist proposes another direction altogether: creativity rooted not in speculative futures but in sustained engagement with living musical heritage and the political urgency of the present. That shift is immediately audible. If Mutate revolved around the Egyptian maqsoum rhythm, this EP opens its vocabulary to rhythmic traditions and performance practices from across the Arab world. The opening “Habban” takes its name from the Gulf bagpipe, a celebratory folk instrument associated with communal dancing and percussion ensembles. Rather than sampling tradition as an exotic signifier, Abadir absorbs its rhythmic logic into a contemporary club framework where darbuka, khishba, mijwiz and intricate hand-clapping patterns become structural rather than decorative elements. The ecstatic propulsion of “The Primitivist” and the playful destabilisation of “Pass & Go” continue that trajectory, while the closing “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” knowingly acknowledges — and moves beyond — the rhythmic strategy that defined his previous album. What remains constant throughout Abadir’s catalogue is his concern with transformation. Each record asks a different question, yet all are linked by the same compositional impulse: taking existing sonic materials — speech, liturgy, social media, club music or regional traditions — and discovering how they can be reimagined without losing their historical or cultural specificity. The result is music that consistently resists easy categorisation. It is uncompromisingly contemporary, yet never relies on futurist rhetoric to justify its newness. In an electronic music landscape still eager to describe unfamiliar sounds as “futuristic,” The Primitivist offers a persuasive alternative. It suggests that innovation need not emerge from imagined worlds or technological fantasies. Sometimes it begins by listening more closely to the present and to histories that have always been there, waiting to be heard. photo by Omar Elkafrawy To helps us see beyond the future, we reached out directly to Abadir. The Primitivist presents itself as a rejection of electronic music’s long-standing fascination with futurism. You’ve argued that futurist narratives often reflect Eurocentric ideas of progress while overlooking the lived realities of communities experiencing war or authoritarianism. Once you reject futurism as the dominant framework, what new possibilities does “primitivism” open up for composition? Does it change the way you think about rhythm, sound design or even the social function of club music? My rejection of anything related to futurism has been going for five years, and each year it becomes more radical. I think this makes sense to me at the moment, since the future, futurism and the futuristic have been the main focus in electronic music since the 80’s (if not even before that) to identify what’s new, what’s next and the unheard for the western ears. This narrative of futurism has been already ruling for 40 years, which makes it outdated for me and repetitive to the maximum, to the point where it’s now reduced to a marketing label. It became a habit to link newness to the future, and unfortunately there has been a lack of critique to this idea, or attempts to link creativity and newness to something else other than futurism. It’s even nostalgic that futurism in electronic music is still somehow based on the same concepts, sounds and perspectives that once existed in the 80’s or the 90’s. There have been cycles of criticizing Mark Fisher’s theories, with a general claim that the future didn’t stop and “gotcha Fisher you are wrong”, because X or Y (from the global north) made “futuristic” music. Honestly, this argument is haunted by an outdated vision of what futuristic music means, it’s also haunted by the urge of futurism. That’s nostalgia for futurism (which is different from Fisher’s concept of lost futures) that used to exist decades ago. It’s paradoxical, and in that sense futurism is eating itself. But I think this sort of discussion doesn’t fit the Arabic context because we have different realities and priorities. With the exception of Afrofuturism, the futuristic narrative is escapist and out of touch with the present. It chooses progress and speed rather than understanding and facing the present. The narrative for years has been about fetishising dystopia or the other opposite, techno-optimism led by the “punchline” of “Let’s imagine a future where…” I see both narratives out of touch with reality, especially now. Being able to think like that is a kind of luxury, rather than living the hard present reality which is unfolding in front of our eyes on a daily basis. So at least, an action must be taken to change that, and actions happen in the present. Once we reach a point where present issues are kind of fixed, then we can have the time and luxury to speculate, think about the future and imagine it. More thoughts about this topic can be found in this essay I wrote last year. I chose the term Primitivism as a provocation, a way to say I’m happy I’m not futuristic, I’m busy with the present and I’m inspired by a deeply rooted music heritage. This way of thinking is definitely inspiring because making this claim means that I need to listen, revisit, read and learn a lot about music from the Arab region on the technical, cultural and historical level. During the last few years I learned a lot about Maqamat, rhythms from different parts of the Arab region. As you said, this also had an impact on sound design, because you can easily tell that the sound design in The Primitivist and my coming project is different from what’s in Kitbashing and Ison. On Mutate, the maqsoum rhythm acted almost as the album’s organising principle, whereas The Primitivist draws from a much broader range of rhythmic traditions and instrumental references from Iraq, Kuwait, Syria and Palestine. Tracks such as “Habban”, “The Primitivist” and “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” feel less concerned with hybridising genres than with rethinking the vocabulary of club music itself. How did your compositional approach change between these two records, and did moving beyond maqsoum also change the way you thought about rhythm? Usually I tend to link my projects together, as well as old and fresh ideas. What starts as a sound or an idea in one project will be revisited and developed more a few years later. You can trace that between Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat and Kitbashing or Ison, and between Mutate and The Primitivist. This marks the continuity of my work. Maqsoum was the center of Mutate, next to the influence of other club genres that I listen to and DJ. I wasn’t making club music before Mutate, so it made sense to me to start with a sound I’m familiar with and stuck in my memory, which is Maqsoum. It was fun mixing Jungle and Footwork or Jersey with sped up and cut up Maqsoum samples, to come up with a mutated club sound. In The Primitivist I decided to focus more on Arabic rhythms and dropping the influences of other club genres. During a 3 year period I got attracted to sounds from the countries you mentioned and I extended my knowledge to further other rhythmic patterns. The result was working with rhythmic sounds related to Dahhiya, Dabke, simulating a real drummer playing the Khishba or using the Sharbaka, which is a hand clapping technique rooted in the Arabian Gulf, especially in Kuwait. In my coming project, I’m going deeper in sound design, and more complex patterns with a focus on variations in time signatures. There is a striking tension throughout the EP between recognisable Arab instruments—mijwiz pipes, darbuka, khishba, brass timbres—and an approach to rhythm and sound design that remains uncompromisingly contemporary. As someone who has also been exploring Arabic maqamat and instrumental playing techniques in your more recent work, how do you avoid turning these traditions into cultural signifiers or markers of authenticity, allowing them instead to remain living musical materials? I think the idea is about avoiding orientalist and self-orientalist cliches, or lazy fusion, in addition to finding this common ground between the familiar and the unfamiliar, with surprise elements. Once you hear a Mijwiz or a brass synth for instance, you will get that sense of “yes I know that”, then twisting the expectations is the next crucial step. If I hear a Rast or Huzam or Bayati maqam used by an Arabic producer, I will see it as normal. But creativity appears depending on some other factors such as: the articulation and ornamentation in maqamat, the modulation between maqamat, how the producer is implementing these maqamat with drum patterns, how the sound design is made, how the arrangement is done and the structure is built. Here you have a lot of options to twist the expectations. Yet, I still admire the musicians who are maintaining old traditions as they are, because we need that now in our region more than any time before, given the external threat by the infamous pariah state, liberal capitalist “values”, A.I, the Dubaification of our region. This is the very material reality we face and we have to deal with in the present, so again, what future exactly are we talking about? Koleyet El Banat – photo by Omar Elkafrawy Your work sits at an unusual intersection of artistic practice and critical writing. As the editor of the electronic music section at Ma3azef, you’re constantly analysing how electronic music is written about, categorised and historicised. Has writing criticism changed the way you make music? Conversely, has producing records like The Primitivist made you more critical of the vocabulary and frameworks through which electronic music — particularly music from the Arab world — is discussed in western publications? My criticism towards the vocabulary and frameworks used in western publications as well as the westernised Arabic ones has always been there. I also believe that the music journalist or the critic has to read, follow and listen a lot, a good level of curiosity is required. I’m trying to do my best with that, so my critique can have some basis. Maybe The Primitivist is a result of that. It’s about how to express critique through a medium other than writing; proposing that we don’t need to be obsessed with the future or futurism to be creative, alternatively, we can be focused in the present or we can draw inspiration from our cultural roots. The present is here already. The same applies on Kitbashing by the way, one can theorise about its concept in an essay or a book, but I wanted to represent the concept sonically. Definitely, working in criticism has made me think differently about my own music, because it has made me much more self-critical. My music projects are slow cooked, and each one starts with a simple question: why am I doing this or what am I trying to say? This question can be frustrating or provocative to some artists, but for me it makes total sense and it’s the main critical question behind every project.ِ During the process, I can be very critical and harsh towards myself, but it helps me a lot. With Kitbashing, you proposed feeding on the algorithm rather than feeding it, transforming the sounds of social media into compositional material. In retrospect, do you think the algorithm can ever truly be subverted, or does every attempt at resisting it inevitably become another form of participation? On an individual level, we can benefit from the algorithm, whether by using it for learning purposes, an introduction to something, being informed about cultural or political topics, or simply watching something fun, because we need a break. Apart from that, ِI wish in general that the algorithm is subverted for something good and I think this has to be collectively done. Take for instance the non-commercial electronic music scene which is now driven by the algorithmic scrolling mentality, everyone from the curators, to the spaces, to the artists, to the press, to the crowd, is so invested in an app. Everything has been highly dependent on Instagram. It has become the main way to be heard and seen and that’s exhausting and frustrating. A couple of slides or a polished one minute video from the peak of a live or DJ set defines an artist. But imagine that the press and curators are relatively withdrawing from Instagram, this can have a good impact on producers and DJs, they will spend less time on the app, and post less, only when it’s necessary. This will make the crowd spend more time listening and reading, and artists will only focus on their music and their work. That would be ideal, isn’t it? (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: Abadir在这张EP中明确挑战电子乐对'未来主义'的执迷，转而深入挖掘阿拉伯世界丰富的活态音乐传统。开篇曲《Habban》以海湾地区庆典用风笛命名，将darbuka、khishba、mijwiz等传统乐器及拍手节奏模式融入俱乐部框架，使其成为结构核心而非异域点缀。整张作品延续Abadir一贯的转化逻辑——对既有声音素材进行重新想象，同时保留其历史文化特异性。从节奏策略到政治批判，《The Primitivist》提出了一种替代路径：创新不必来自想象世界或技术幻梦，而是源于对当下与传统更细致的聆听。评论文字详尽深入，涵盖概念阐释与音乐分析，论据充分。

items.body: Cuban drummer Francisco Mela’s free jazz odyssey continues on four new releases, writes Daniel Spicer in The Wire 512 Francisco Mela Carnaval De Oriente 577 CD/DL Jowee Omicil & Francisco Mela OM BasH! Village DL Rafael Zaldivar Zaldivar/McBride/Mela: Meeting In New York Vol 1 577 DL Matthew Putman/Hill Greene/Francisco Mela Bright Sun Outside 577 CD/DL Cuban drummer Francisco Mela’s route into the mysteries of free jazz has been a circuitous one. He started out as a teenager working in the bands of Latin jazz pianists and fellow countrymen Emiliano Salvador and Gabriel Hernandez before moving to the US at the turn of the millennium and building a reputation as an in-demand straightahead jazz drummer, playing with Joe Lovano and enjoying nearly a decade in pianist McCoy Tyner’s trio. Following Tyner’s death in 2020 and the forced hiatus of the pandemic, Mela emerged with a new fascination for and commitment to freedom, forging a fruitful partnership with the Brooklyn based 577 label and collaborating with heavy-hitters including William Parker, Cooper-Moore and Matthew Shipp. His journey is not entirely without precedent. Milford Graves cut his teeth in the early 1960s playing congas and timbales in Latin and Afro-Cuban outfits and led The Milford Graves Latino Quartet, featuring a young pianist by the name of Chick Corea, before a 1962 encounter with the volcanic eruptions of Elvin Jones alongside Tyner in John Coltrane’s quartet inspired him to turn to the drum kit and become a key architect of the mid-60s free jazz New Thing, entirely rewiring the possibilities of time and timbre in the process. In Cuban pianist Rafael Zaldivar’s trio, Mela teams up with Christian McBride, who held bass duties in Corea’s trio with drummer Brian Blade, as heard on the 2013 live album Trilogy. In fact, on Meeting In New York Vol 1, Zaldivar at times channels a strikingly similar feel to Corea’s sophisticated and sentimental tunefulness, embraced by McBride’s muscular lyricism. It’s a temptation Mela resolutely resists, avoiding Blade’s deep swing in favour of a constant flickering fizz of cymbals and snare, dancing playfully around the idea of time. At other moments, Zaldivar summons puckish declamations more akin to Paul Bley, eliciting a brawnier churn from Mela punctuated by sudden gunshot snare cracks while, in a diaphanous free ballad, his subtle brush work shushes and sighs in gaseous textures. Here, McBride – not often heard in a free context – sounds a little out of place, cramming as many notes as possible into solos perhaps more suited to a contemporary post-bop milieu. There’s no such mismatch in the trio with pianist Matthew Putman, where the low end is held down by Hilliard Greene, a bassist with considerable avant garde credentials, having worked with the likes of pianists Don Pullen and Cecil Taylor, and saxophonist Charles Gayle. Bright Sun Outside navigates more familiar free jazz terrain and isn’t afraid to ramble. Even some of its fairly brief improvisations, lasting just a few minutes, convey a sense of loose and leisurely meandering, with Putman flicking out spontaneous melodic gambits that seem quite content to never fully commit to a destination – like a succession of half-formed thoughts bubbling up in an unhurried internal monologue. Mela is happily along for the ride, laying out a rattling commentary dominated by an arrestingly dry snare, each stroke deftly placed with neat precision. When Greene leans into rasping arco shrieks and Putman chops out sudden staccato stabs, Mela flexes his muscles with a more aggressive energy, like fresh flames springing up from glowing embers. Mela’s first solo album Carnaval De Oriente proposes a wholly different mood. Inspired by the sounds of the eponymous street carnival heard in his childhood, he rolls around the drum kit – revealing a loose, earthy sound reminiscent of Graves – adding shakers, cowbell and sundry percussion. All the while, he chirps spontaneous vocal chants and snatches of song that recall percussionist/vocalist Juno Lewis’s mythically resonant Afro-Creole vocals on his song “Kulu Sé Mama (Juno Sé Mama)”, recorded with John Coltrane in 1965. On one track, Mela tinkers with rudimentary innocence on a glockenspiel; on another, he picks clumsily at an acoustic guitar. What he lacks in chops, he makes up for with unabashed enthusiasm. Whistling absentmindedly and chatting contentedly to himself, he sounds like he’s having a fine time. When the full kit breaks through in a burst of dense polyrhythms, you can pretty much hear the smile on his face. His concise improvised duets with Canadian-Haitian multi-instrumentalist Jowee Omicil are in a similar vein, as the pair explore the shared musical traditions of Haiti and Cuba. On saxophones and clarinet, Omicil displays some of the loquacious unpredictability of Eric Dolphy, while Mela rolls out a nimble undertow that occasionally comes close to a standard jazz sound, replete with full-bodied rolls and tumbles. Omicil’s lip-smacking pocket trumpet works Mela up into a frenzied freakout of ecstatic vocal cries. Intuitive piano splashes invite a thoughtful drizzle of snare and ride. Mela sings with lusty abandon and thwacks out hambone rhythms on his own body. Again, a palpable sense of spontaneous joy reigns throughout. There’s an obvious similarity to Don Cherry’s duets with drummer Ed Blackwell, as documented on the twin Mu albums: while reaching back past the dim origins of jazz, Mela and Omicil conduct imaginary Pangaean rituals bursting with the same omnivorous exuberance that colours all of Mela’s music. This review appears in The Wire 512 along with many other reviews of new and recent records, books, films, festivals and more. To read them all, pick up a copy of the magazine in our online shop. Wire subscribers can also read the issue in our online magazine library.

items.body: This ensemble will always carry a deeply personal connotation for me. In 2015, they released their first album, Rune , at a time when I was hospitalised for two weeks, waking at irregular hours. Despite the dire circumstances, listening to Earth Tongues at four in the morning, alone in the darkness, was a strange and deeply soothing experience. There was something about the ensemble’s careful, almost cautious little sounds—the tiny sonic points that gradually accumulated into a landscape that absorbed, captivated, and ultimately elevated you—that created a uniquely powerful listening experience. It is difficult to explain how important it became for me to return to this music again and again, and how much it taught me about the value of life, the value of art, and the value of improvised music. When everything collapses around you—and inside you—you begin to realise that whatever remains, however small or fragmented, can still be enough to create something meaningful. You learn to cherish the smallest isolated event - " at least I still have this ", to pay attention to what might otherwise go unnoticed, and to welcome the spontaneous connections with and between people who can, together, create beauty out of those tiny fragments of luck. And in many ways, that is what this music does. Little sounds, little fragments, little pieces surrounded by silence, which, when brought together, can still constitute something beautiful, something meaningful, something valuable. It gave me hope against all odds, and with it a profound insight: to cherish every moment. Life is not necessarily a long story with a clear plot. Perhaps it is instead a collection of small, random events—fragments that, taken together, become a life, and that are all worth living. The trio, so many years later are still Joe Moffett on trumpet, Dan Peck on tuba, and Carlo Costa on percussion. Like their previous albums, their sound is deeply organic, drawing on the textures and rhythms of the natural world: the drip of water, pebbles falling, animals growling, birds twittering. Each of the three long tracks has its own distinct character, while the music gradually evolves from pointillist blips into increasingly stretched-out tones in the final piece. Very slowly, almost imperceptibly, these scattered sonic fragments begin to coalesce. The subtlety of this shift is deliberate, shaped by carefully considered compositional ideas and structures. Silence is an essential part of their music—the white space between colours, an open realm of possibility waiting to be filled. What makes their work so compelling is the extraordinary value they give to each individual sound, with an intense attention to precision, texture, and timbral quality. When you enter their music attentively, it seems to slow down rational thought itself, allowing you to surrender to the sound and, for a while, simply be the music. Listen and download from Bandcamp . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: Earth Tongues 是一支由小号、图巴和打击乐组成的三重奏，2026年发行专辑《Phases》，延续了2015年首作《Rune》以来的创作路线。专辑包含三首长篇作品，音乐从点彩式的微小声响出发，逐步演变为拉长的持续音，自然声音如水滴、碎石、鸟鸣被融入有机质感中。三位乐手以极其精确的方式赋予每一个声音独立价值，关注音色质地与织体层次。沉默作为构图要素贯穿始终，为声音提供呼吸空间。整体结构经过精心设计，碎片化的音响在缓慢演变中逐渐汇聚成型，要求聆听者以专注状态进入，让理性思维减速，使听者暂时成为音乐本身。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张九碟套装回顾了韩国音乐家Jin Hi Kim四十年来的录音作品，跨越她从韩国传统音乐转向电子音乐与即兴创作的旅程。专辑由独立厂牌Neuma发行，以五张碟收录管弦乐与室内乐作品，四张碟记录与Gerry Hemingway、Susie Ibarra、Tony Oxley、Bill Frisell等不同领域音乐人的即兴合作。最为独特的是Kim对传统玄琴（komungo）的革新——通过计算机接口与信号处理，将这件四世纪以来的五尺长鲁特琴的音色范围大幅扩展，赋予其冥想性的内在能量。作品横跨图形记谱、跨文化移植、电子声学实验等多种路径，既有早期用西方乐器转译韩国音乐的尝试，也有与顶级即兴大师的对话，展现出持续探索的勇气与多样性。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦四张即兴录音作品，跨越十二年，探讨集体即兴创作中"同时书写"与"近距离聆听"所形成的深层对话。评论者将这类音乐描述为可穿越语言与意义壁垒的声响，介于已知与未知之间，兼具神秘感与美感。文章着重介绍Emilio Gordoa与已故Sven-Åke Johansson的二重奏专辑《Die Dritte Ebene》，录音于2023年8月。两位音乐家的演奏呈现出透明度极高的平行线条，从中涌现出某种"第三层"——接近幽灵般的神秘存在。专辑使人联想到Erik Satie的家具音乐，重复材料的特殊共鸣营造出近乎出神的状态，在两人声部之间生成一种反思性的意识空间，既具启发性又带有催眠特质。

A rusting Weltschmerz bleeds through Darren Cunningham’s music, dissolving evanescent motifs into lasting affect. Over twenty years into his career, Radical Frame sees the UK producer continue to explore music that resists forgetting. The almost preternatural allure of Cunningham’s first proper solo... items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是英国制作人Darren Cunningham重返Ninja Tune厂牌的作品。评论指出，其音乐难以用旋律或节奏记忆，而是一种黑色电影般的氛围感知——凌晨四点独自穿行于城市雾气中的感官印象。钢琴短促的刺探声贯穿于汹涌的音色浪潮与氛围织体之间，转瞬即逝的动机溶解为持久的情绪效果。专辑延续了Cunningham二十余年职业生涯中对'抗拒遗忘'之声音的探索，首张正式个人作品展现出超越寻常的神秘吸引力。整体呈现出低保真电子、环境音乐与IDM的融合特质，声音设计偏向实验性氛围营造，适合深夜聆听。

items.body: “The Gray” is the second album by Italian producer Stefano Santi. Four years after his debut album, “JXDY”, the artist draws inspiration from themes such as love, loss, and collapse. He has also enlisted guest vocalists including Meldamor, Castelli, Contre Soirée, and Filmmaker. “The Gray” features a diverse range of influences—sometimes further accentuated by the guest vocalists—yet the album maintains a strong sense of cohesion. The opening track is brilliant, sounding like Shoegaze with subtle Dark-Wave undertones. These two influences remain prominent and, to my ears, constitute the album’s most compelling elements. However, you will also discover touches of Dream-Pop and even a more Dance-oriented track featuring Meldamor. The vocals are produced in a distinctive way, hovering in the background like a mist settling over the songs while still making their mark. Musically, I find the guitar work superb, particularly on the tracks leaning towards Shoegaze. Synth arrangements are also incorporated, at times heightening the atmosphere while adding a fresh dimension to the overall sound. The final track is an instrumental that feels like an outro, but one of exceptional quality. It stands out as a highlight in terms of atmosphere and provides a powerful conclusion to an album filled with gems. “The Gray” is a fantastic record that sounds like a distinctive fusion of several closely related genres. Definitely worth checking out! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Hxlding Time”: Hxlding Time by Never About Never Never is the solo project of Italian producer Stefano Santi, based in Milan. The project debuted with the album “JXDY” on 18 March 2022 (catalog VEYL033) on the Veyl label, recorded as instinct-led material that was not originally planned as a full-length. Santi’s first outside collaboration was a remix of Years Of Denial‘s “City Lights”, a step that carried into his second album, “The Gray”, released via Veyl on 26 June 2026 (catalog VEYL048) and built around guest contributions including Arizona duo Meldamor.
items._cn_summary: 意大利制作人Stefano Santi以Never为名发布的第二张专辑《The Gray》围绕爱、失去与崩塌等主题展开，邀请Meldamor、Castelli等客座人声参与。整张作品在Shoegaze音墙与Darkwave冷暗质感之间游走，同时点缀Dream-Pop氛围与一首更具舞曲色彩的合作曲目。人声被刻意推入背景，如薄雾笼罩于器乐之上，却仍清晰可辨。吉他层次尤为突出，合成器编排则在多处强化空间感与情绪厚度。终曲以纯器乐形式收束，如同一段高质量的Outro，在氛围营造上达到全专高点。发行厂牌Veyl为独立电子/暗潮领域的小众标签，整张作品在类型融合上展现出明确的个人审美与统一性。

items.body: On the cotton candy sky Written every moment of life For all eternity Wonder why we are even alive Some records come from a scene, some from a city, and some seem to come from that ugly five-minute interval after you have stared at your phone too long and suddenly hate civilization. Faded Flowers, the latest album from Turkish Darkwave duo Ductape, belongs to the third category. It looks around at modern life: crowded rooms, digital selves, obedient routines, private disintegration, and finds a species that has become astonishingly good at maintaining appearances while quietly running itself into the ground. Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray formed Ductape in 2019 in Istanbul, where their mix of post-punk, darkwave, Turkish and English lyrics quickly carried them well beyond the usual underground boundaries. Four albums and two EPs later, they have relocated their creative base to France. Geography changes; the unease travels well. On Faded Flowers, that unease has acquired a larger target. The title gives you the central image without turning it into homework: people as flowers left too long beneath bad light, drained by repetition, expectation, isolation, and the exhausting business of becoming whatever the surrounding machinery finds acceptable. You can hear that pressure everywhere. The basslines have the cold discipline of public transport at six in the morning. Synthesizers cut through with little sympathy. Furkan’s guitar keeps finding ways to sound agitated without becoming decorative, sometimes stalking around Çağla’s voice, sometimes answering it, sometimes scraping at the walls. Çağla’s magnificent voice remains the great destabilizing force in Ductape. She can sound detached enough to frighten you, then suddenly let some exposed nerve show through before the song has time to make a ceremony of it. There is very little comfort in that delivery, which suits an album concerned with the absurdity of living among millions of people and still feeling marooned. That particular contradiction runs all through Faded Flowers. Everyone is visible now. Everyone is reachable. Everyone is encouraged to construct a public version of themselves, polish it, post it, improve it, defend it, sell it, then wake up tomorrow and do the same miserable maintenance all over again. Somewhere along the line, identity became administrative labour. Ductape sounds thoroughly fed up with the arrangement. The album keeps circling the false authorities people submit to without necessarily believing in them: social roles, digital identities, manufactured ideals, systems of power, inherited expectations, all those little invisible rules that become oppressive mostly because nobody remembers agreeing to them. There is anger in these songs, but also exhaustion, and the exhaustion may be more interesting. Rage still assumes you have energy to spare. Fine considers one dubious convenience of hitting bottom: at least you can stop pretending the view is lovely. The album’s first single follows a collapse through pain and disorientation toward an unexpected sense of ownership, as Çağla finds a place for herself inside the very circumstances that have undone her. A steady bassline and luminous synthesizers carry her weary composure, giving that uneasy acceptance room to develop. There is something wonderfully suspect about feeling comfortable down there, and the song lets the suspicion sit beside the relief. Within an album preoccupied with keeping up appearances, surrendering the performance becomes its own small freedom. The accompanying black-and-white video turns that process into a homemade alchemical experiment. Filmed at Misuc in Ankara, it casts the duo as silent-film experimenters collecting ingredients and tending a potion among curious specimens. Ductape handled the direction, styling, and production, with camera work by Mert Yalçın and editing by Çağla Güleray. Its antique laboratory makes an apt workshop for two people attempting to assemble another version of themselves. Standout track Obscure moves with a bassline so blunt and heavy it seems capable of carrying the song by itself, while Furkan Güleray’s distorted guitar keeps worrying at the edges, leaving abrasions rather than decoration. Synths hang overhead with an icy, almost antiseptic quality, giving the music the uneasy stillness of a room where something unpleasant has already been said. Çağla Güleray sings in English, her low register remarkably composed as she picks through disillusionment without dressing it up for sympathy. That restraint makes the words hit harder. Stolen light, dead idols, resentment calcified through repetition, the dull vacancy that follows years of believing in something that eventually reveals itself as another instrument of control: Obscure gathers these ideas until the song begins to feel less like despair than the slow recognition of how thoroughly faith can be exploited. There is damage here, certainly, but also the uncomfortable clarity that comes when the old explanations have finally stopped working. Its Berlin performance video brings that severity onto the stage. Directed by Altay Erlik, with cinematography by Emrah Celik and laser animation by Peter Isachenko, the clip concentrates on the duo’s physical presence, giving the song’s accusations the directness of an encounter across a crowded room. On Gölgesiz, the effort of continuing becomes almost physical. Sung in Turkish, the album’s second single carries accumulated sorrow through persistent drums and guitar figures that seem caught in the same argument with themselves. Çağla keeps her delivery measured, making fatigue audible through the weight she gives each phrase. The rhythm maintains its appointment with the next bar while the person inside it struggles to find a reason to follow. That uneasy relationship between bodily momentum and emotional depletion gives the song its force, extending the album’s concern with lives organised around obligations that have outlasted their meaning. Made during Ductape’s Latin American tour, the monochrome DIY video places Çağla against expanses of water and open space, her figure often reduced to a silhouette. Visual distortions make her outline appear unstable, as though even occupying a body has become difficult work. The images give the song’s isolation a scale that the surrounding emptiness only enlarges. Faded Flowers gains its pull from the sense that decay is something social as much as personal. The individual breaks down because the surrounding structure is already cracked. The city keeps moving. The screen keeps glowing. The machine keeps asking for another password. Somewhere inside all that, a person still has to decide who they are. Ductape leave that question open, with the bass still moving underneath it. Listen to Faded Flowers below and order the album here. Faded Flowers by Ductape To celebrate the album release, Ductape have announced headline shows and festival dates across Europe well into 2027. items._cn_summary: 土耳其二人组Ductape的第四张专辑以'枯萎的花朵'为核心意象，审视现代人在数字身份、社会角色与权力规训中的缓慢瓦解。贝斯线如清晨六点公共交通般冷峻克制，合成器毫不留情地切入，Furkan的吉他始终处于躁动与装饰性的临界点，缠绕或回应Çağla那极具不稳定感的声线——她能在疏离与暴露之间瞬间切换，不给歌曲留任何仪式化的余地。专辑反复环绕那些人们服从却未必相信的虚假权威：社会角色、数字自我、制造的理想、继承的期待。愤怒之下更耐人寻味的是疲惫，因为愤怒至少假设你还有多余的力气。整张作品捕捉了'身处百万人群仍觉流离失所'这一当代悖论，融合土耳其与英语歌词的实践也为这张以欧洲为创作基地的暗潮作品带来独特的地理与文化位移。

items.body: Happy golden anniversary to the International Computer Music Conference! This special album honors founder David Wessel (1942–2014). The full title of the 2025 theme: Curiosity, Play, Innovation—A 50th Anniversary Celebration of Creativity in Music, Science and Technology. This generous collection showcases electro-acoustic music from around the world. Each piece is intricate and unique, while many touch upon contemporary themes, starting with Jiajing Zhao‘s “Glitchopolis,” a commentary on information overload. The very first sound is that of an alarm, doubled and then tripled, set against London traffic, which begins to fracture, stutter and glitch. Garbled human voices emerge from a processed vat; construction and technology intertwine. A bee – real and metaphoric – buzzes by, followed by a flock of birds, fireworks and a police siren. How many inputs can one brain handle? “Pardon me, ‘scuse me, sorry,” a commuter apologizes at the end. By refusing to mute the signals, the composer imitates the feeling of being overwhelmed, not only aural, but emotionally. “Rumors, approximated” by Shane Turner with Simone Pitot (Delorca) uses algorithms to translate sound into data. The textures are the key, but as patterns emerge, questions of value arise: are these patterns authentic or unintentional? And how much of the human remains after technology has had its say? While Pitot purposely subjected her vocals to this process, other parts of life are unwittingly fed to the whims of the machine. Zeo Lin‘s Escape, whose opening minutes flirt with the dance floor, is filled with glass crashes and computer beeps, percussion and synth, piano and breath, representing a clash between the organic and the electronic, its movements marked by the click of a cassette. At the end a church bell tolls, only to by subsumed by static. Daniele Valenti‘s “CAN you hear them?” is particularly clever, derived almost entirely from the timbres of cans. Without knowing this, one might only guess at the nature of these sounds. The knowledge allows one to lean in,, to cherish the sounds made by the humble object that one often kicks down the road or discards without any attention to its aural qualities. Can a can sound like traffic, or rain? Yes, it CAN. In contrast, “Hammerklavier” uses the piano as its acoustic source, with Antonio Argentieri doing pretty much everything but playing the keys. Think of Matmos’ Ultimate Care II, which performed a similar feat with a washing machine. Few would ever guess that this is a piano piece, which exponentially increases its appeal. How does it feel to be “an international student with limited English proficiency” in London? Hongquan Yang and Fan Zu attempt to translate the experience in “Rambling,” starting with a traditional classroom speech about sound, then feeding it through echo, loop and reverb, injecting their own language to return the favor. Soon everyone is confused, yet finds common ground in the tempo and the playful approach. Passing grade! The chimes and choral tones of the beautifully titled “A Poem for Little Things” turn out to have been taken from children’s toys; as the mother of twins, Chung Eun Kim‘s aural environment has been altered, and she has responded by altering it right back, finding rhythm and melody, wonder and awe, in a castanet, maraca or toy xylophone. “Decorate beauty” is the concept behind Peter Dickson Lopez and Ensemble MISE-EN. “Mise En Series I” begins as a pure chamber piece before the electro-acoustic elements enter; the timbre approaches drone, as the instruments swell with sound, underpinned by pensive electronics. As if coming full cycle, Liu Yurai‘s “The Shackle” is inspired by a visit to the thousand-year-old Daci Temple, an oasis of peace located in the heart of Chengdu. The contrast between peace and overload (as first addressed in “Glitchopolis”) is palpable. Tapping and texting sounds overlap and threaten to undo all calm; a train clacks by; passengers chatter. Soon the bicycle bells are replaced by temple bells, the incoherent conversations with chants, the traffic with birdsong, and a sense of balance is restored. Unfortunately, albeit realistically, the outside world keeps rushing back in. “Seascape Serenity” readjusts the scene. Yu Chia Kuo and SinYu Deng pack the soundscape with hydrophone recordings that reflect the ecosystems of Taiwan. Just as one wished for the serenity of the temple in “The Shackle,” one wishes for humans to stop polluting the biophony of this piece. And yet, this is part of the lesson: that marine life is at least as stressed as we are and that we have caused both. While the piece attempts a happy ending, increasing the number of species calls, one wonders how realistic this might be; the title becomes less a reflection of the piece than an elegy. Taken as a whole, Best of the Listening Rooms demonstrates incredible range while managing to flow beautifully as a whole. The collection is sociologically enlightening yet retains a sense of fun, honoring the theme. Most couples are winding down by their golden anniversary, but we have a feeling that the International Computer Music Conference is just getting started. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑为国际计算机音乐会议五十周年纪念合集，致敬创始人David Wessel，收录来自全球的电子声学作品。赵嘉静的《Glitchopolis》以警报声、伦敦交通噪音和破碎的故障效果模拟信息过载的感官体验。Shane Turner与Delorca合作的《Rumors, approximated》将人声通过算法转化为数据纹理，探讨技术与人类主体性之间的张力。Zeo Lin的《Escape》在舞曲节奏与玻璃碎裂、磁带咔哒声之间游走，结尾以静态吞噬教堂钟声收束。Daniele Valenti的《CAN you hear them?》几乎完全由罐头声源构成，看似平凡的物体却能模拟交通与雨声。Antonio Argentieri的《Hammerklavier》则将钢琴作为纯粹的声学素材进行非常规处理，几乎无法辨认其原始乐器身份。整张专辑将日常声音、数字处理与作曲意图编织成对当代听觉经验的多元反思。

items.body: For all its stunning virtuosity, the tumbling fingerstyle guitar of Swedish guitarist Finn Loxbo is always in service to a set of brilliant compositional ideas Digging through the various improvised solo and duo recordings Swedish guitarist Finn Loxbo has made over the last decade is like witnessing a slow-motion creative winnowing, observing how a feverish pile of ideas and experiments has gradually coalesced into something inscrutable. His third solo album Lummernikt is a work of astonishing focus and originality forged from familiar notions, a free improvisation practice patiently chiseled into compositional rigour. Across eight riveting acoustic pieces played live without overdubs, Loxbo melds extended technique, fingerstyle fluency and self-devised preparations to deliver one of the year’s most beguiling, detailed and beautiful... items._cn_summary: 瑞典吉他手 Finn Loxbo 的第三张个人专辑收录了八首原声作品，全部现场录制、无叠录。评论指出，他过去十年的即兴独奏与二重奏录音逐渐从繁杂的实验走向高度凝练的作曲结构，呈现出惊人的专注力与原创性。在指弹技巧之外，他运用扩展技法与自制乐器准备，将自由即兴的实践耐心雕琢为严格的作曲框架。整张专辑以熟悉的原声吉他为载体，却承载着极为密集的作曲构思与层次丰富的声响探索，在极简编制中实现了对技术与结构的双重推进。

As I listened to the tracks, I felt as if I were taking a journey around the world?and then even farther, into the Universe.There are subtle folk motifs that seem to echo Slavic heritage, intertwined with oriental influences and sounds that somehow touch the rhythm of the heartbeat. The combination creates a feeling of movement, discovery, and something almost timeless.
items.body: Review by ElenaNL — The music is simply amazing. This album feels quite different from the other music by Compassionizer. As I listened to the tracks, I felt as if I were taking a journey around the world?and then even farther, into the Universe.There are subtle folk motifs that seem to echo Slavic heritage, intertwined with oriental influences and sounds that somehow touch the rhythm of the heartbeat. The combination creates a feeling of movement, discovery, and something almost timeless.I'm a dreamer by nature, and I love to "travel" through time, imagine distant places, and create worlds that don't exist anywhere except in my imagination. The music on this album feels like a perfect companion for that kind of journey. It doesn't simply fill the background?it guides the dreams, opens space for deep thoughts, and gives the imagination somewhere to wander.The vocals are a beautiful addition to the overall experience. They add another layer to the music without taking away from its atmospheric and almost cinematic quality.What I especially appreciate is the feeling the album leaves behind. It doesn't feel heavy or overwhelming, and there is no unpleasant aftertaste or excessive excitement. Instead, it leaves me with a sense of freshness, as if my mind has been gently cleared and filled with new thoughts.Each track feels like a small story of its own, with its own characters, atmosphere, journey, and ending. Together, the tracks create something that feels like a collection of little worlds?each one inviting you to step inside for a while and see where it takes you.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以跨界前卫摇滚为骨架，融合斯拉夫民间元素与东方色彩的音乐动机，营造出环球漫游乃至星际遨游的听觉旅程。每首曲目各自构建独立的小型叙事场景，拥有专属的氛围与情感弧线，连缀成一部微型世界集合。人声作为增添的层次融入整体，既不破坏氛围化的电影感铺陈，也强化了作品的叙事深度。整体音乐不流于沉重或过度亢奋，听后留下的是清爽与思绪被重新梳理的余韵，既适合作为梦境与想象的引导，也承载着对时间与远方的好奇心。器乐编排细腻，节奏与心跳律动暗合，呈现出兼具探索性与内省气质的独特声景。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — I know nothing of this artist but I have had many encounters with idiosyncratic creatives like him, so I feel somewhat steeled, if not totally qualified (who is?), for the experience of listening to this album. 1. "I Had a Dream" (2:13) over a recording of a female student's English narration of a dream of hers a NuJazz multi-track weave of multiple horns, synth horns, pianos, xylophones, fuzzy electric guitars, and bass and drums and synthesizer noises all travel together like the start of a marathon race: with each instrument traveling an oscillating path of pitch, all at the same speed, each with their own individual, loose and idiosyncratic expressions of the same directional goal. Interesting. Reminds me of something Markuus Pajakaala would do (especially because of the prominent presence of low-end horns like bassoons or baritone saxophones mixed with multiple tracks of various tuned percussion instruments). (4.375/5)2. "Memories of a Loser" (3:39) a kind of bleed-over from the previous dream song turns into a kind of loose jazz lounge (or airport piano and sundry instruments and sounds that happen to show up--including honking horns from taxis) all given motion by a rolling bass, drums and piano. There are appearances from quite a variety of "passer-by" guests, including multiple horns, all acting as if they're just walking by and happen to have an instrument to throw into the mix for a few seconds before moving on. Interesting. (8.75/10)3. "I Want You (She's So Heavy)" (4:04) Yes, that "I Want You (She's So Heavy)"--here rendered by jazzy-blues-rock combo with a very active drummer, multiple guitar, keyboard/synth, and horn contributors, each throwing their Fred Frith-Sonny Sharrock-like interpretations into the increasingly-wild mix. Interesting. (8.875/10)4. "El lado oscuro de la calle" (3:31) synth- & electric guitar-generated noises, programmed drum/percussion, bass, and Holger Czukay-like random radio-recording tracks fed into the same David Torn/Stephan Thelen/SONAR-like Future Possible Jazz Musics mix. I happen to LOVE this! Sounds like the kind of music a self-assured terrorist might be listening to on his noise-cancelling headphones as he cased out a target airport, train station, bus depot or the like. (9.333/10)5. "The Narrow Way" (3:53) faded in BRAINTICKET-like melody pattern of synth/organ and piano with drums and synth-saw bass line in which voices, field recordings, pianos, keyboards, eerie synthesizers, and other instruments weave in and out of each other's presence with almost violent and reckless abandon despite all somewhat following the rising and falling oscillation of the main bass and synth melody line. (9/10)6. "La m�quina de los sue�os" (3:32) a cool jazz track that could easily occupy a soundtrack to a street-walking scene in a spy movie: there are tons of supplemental tracks woven in and out, panning across the soundscape, a lot of them treated field recordings of radio and/or passers-by voices. Very cool. (9.125/10)7. "Ostinato en Em" (2:36) hypnotic left-hand piano pattern is congested with many other layers of horns, guitars, drums, percussion, more piano tracks, all spewing forth their vomit and excrement like a scene of exhaust plumes flowing thickly into the air from factory smokestacks, all moving synchronously in the same direction, same pattern. Excellent, though I wish it would've morphed or transitioned. (4.625/5)8. "El trapecio" (3:16) jazz drums with descending chord bass line over/within which everything but the kitchen sinks thrown in from the listening drone flying around the airspace outside a busy mega-high-rise apartment complex. Okay as a dumping ground but under-developed. (8.75/10)9. "Onda Media" (3:15) the soundtrack to an hour in the life of an airport's robotic floor cleaner/vacuum, all recorded, filtered through a high-speed playback feature so that the sound and visuals are moving in 3x speed. We're starting to travel beyond the boundaries of what is acceptable as dance and entertainment music: something that would be more appropriate to a 22nd Century Ornette Coleman, John Zorn, or Sonny Sharrock (which is beyond my tolerance or enjoyment capacity). (8.667/10)10. "El final del camino" (2:57) the musical interpretation, capture, and/or expression of the cacophony of modern world mall life? (8.75/10)11."Los platos rotos" (5:15) drums and drones: the first playing free jazz, the second providing stable observer perspective. This one actually grew on me--began making sense as well as achieving NEON HEART-like sublimity for me. Why this one and not some of the others I cannot explain. Perhaps the grounding, pacifying effect of the heavily reverbed Fender Rhodes or dreamy infinity notes coming out of the electric guitars helping to balance/offset the angsty drum play. (9.25/10)12. "Ambient Loser" (1:57) gentle guitar and horn lullaby with glitch percussives. (4.5/5)13. "Carnaval" (3:35) a Latin percussion display with incidental synth-generated noises thrown in every few seconds for spice and futuristic sci-fi effect. Interesting. (8.875/10)Totla Time 43:42I really enjoyed the journey arc through "real" modern world soundscapes that this album took me through. Though there are several songs I would call "keepers"--that I will look forward to when they come up in my random shuffle playlists--a lot of it feels like �tudes or attempts to capture a single emotion or random life situation--which is not wrong or bad, just not universally appealing. B+/4.5 stars; an excellent collection of one artist's personal and very modern perspectives of the world as he sees/experiences it. Some of these often-unusual and hyper-stimulating songs are bound to connect while some are bound to rankle: each listener will experience it differently, according to his/her/their own personal experiences and moods. I do recommend the experience: who knows what you'll get out of it!
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以NuJazz为骨架，将多轨铜管、合成器号角、钢琴、木琴、模糊电吉他、贝斯与鼓机编织成密集而松散并存的声场。各曲均以即兴式的多层次叠加为特征：低音声部的巴松或上低音萨克斯与多调打击乐器构成震荡旋律线，路人式的客串乐器在lounge氛围中随意进出，电台采样与田野录音被混入爵士摇滚结构。评论人多次提及Holger Czukay、David Torn、Fred Frith等实验与前卫爵士参照系，并形容部分段落像恐怖分子在机场踩点时聆听的未来可能爵士音乐。第六曲回归冷爵士基调，辅以大量横移声场的环境录音，可作为间谍电影街巷场景的配乐。整体呈现高度个性化的声音拼贴美学。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Listening to Autobahn, both the album and the title track, one begins to notice just how many artists they have influenced, across both rock and electronic music. The sonic leap from the previous album is immense; there is a minimalist approach, repetition, and layers of sound that are subtly added one by one, like raindrops we don't notice until there are too many of them, and it is these layers that drive the changes.The structure is progressive, evolving even as the same central theme repeats, shifting in timing, speed, and ultimately, meaning. The synthesizers create a vast stereo universe; we were sensing modernity before it had even arrived. Atmospheres and moods were evoked; beneath that veneer of coldness lay substance and emotion, and I am thinking not only of Brian Eno, but also of David Byrne, Magazine, and Ultravox. Suddenly, it feels like a racetrack, and the synthesizers abandon the melody, though not the harmony.The synthesizers then reach a certain symphonic depth, before becoming a sort of religious choir as the electronic drums forever leave behind the mere science fiction of the 50s and 60s. And the Minimoog joins the vocals to create a new melody towards the end, creating within this staging, a certain form of new modern epic."Kometenmelodie 1" is dark and cinematic, with the lead synthesizer contrasting against the delicate piano whispering in the background, allowing the duo of Ralf H�tter and Florian Schneider to shine with their full theatricality."Kometenmelodie 2," on the other hand, is luminous, like its counterpart, representing the two faces of the theater. It once again features the synthesizer-and-keyboard duet, yet here it almost anticipates the modern 80s pop that would later draw upon its lessons. A symphonic-progressive air drifts through, much like that comet, complemented by Wolfgang Fl�r's electronic drums. "Mitternacht" holds echoes that reverberate in an almost ecclesiastical, yet psychedelic, manner; it gradually reveals itself as a musical painting, rich in textures to unravel, dissect, and try to comprehend, or simply to let wash over you and feel.There is something organic about Morgenspaziergang, the sound of the flute and the birds, yet at this point, it is entirely an experience for the senses, a matter of perceiving and surrendering to them. After so much overexposure to technology, and the coldness and concrete of highways and "musique concr�te", it is as if the earth and Kraftwerk are responding, much like their compatriots Popol Vuh, with a return to a certain kind of nature, one whose uniqueness is only revealed after having left it behind. There is nothing more modern than that.
items._cn_summary: Kraftwerk 1974年的《Autobahn》被视为电子音乐史上的里程碑之作。专辑以极简主义手法铺陈，由单一主题反复变奏，速度、节奏与意义层层推进，开创了立体声合成器营造的广阔声场。评论特别提到电子鼓击破了五六十年代科幻音乐的局限，Minimoog与人声交织出新的旋律走向，赋予作品一种现代史诗感。《Kometenmelodie 1》以阴郁的电影质感呈现，《Kometenmelodie 2》则趋向光亮，二者构成戏剧的两面。《Mitternacht》带有教堂回响与迷幻色彩，层次丰富如同音乐画卷。终曲《Morgenspaziergang》以长笛与鸟鸣收束，在工业化冰冷叙事后回归自然，呼应德国同代人 Popol Vuh 的自然回望主题。整张专辑在结构进化、声音实验与跨类型影响方面均具有前瞻意义。
