items.body: Faris Ishaq‘s uncle had got hold of some reed cane from Jericho and asked Faris’s older brother to cut holes in it so he could play it. The brother made the flute. Faris, sixteen at the time, picked it up before his uncle got the chance and kept it. He was four years into euphonium lessons at the Edward Said National Conservatory, but the sound of that homemade nay took hold of him completely. Nobody taught him what to do with it. There was nothing to teach, really: no mouthpiece, no keys, nothing mechanical to explain, just cane, breath, and whatever he could find by trial. Then he saw Dhafer Youssef play live and understood how far it could go. The nay is a Middle Eastern flute with 5,000 years behind it, answering to breath and nothing else. That is either a severe limitation or the entire point, and Ishaq has spent twenty years proving it’s the second. For the fifth episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we follow Faris Ishaq from that room in Bethlehem to Berklee’s Global Jazz programme, where a full scholarship took him and he was named top student for running Arabic maqam through jazz harmony. He has since released three albums, recorded with Grammy-winning bassist John Patitucci, featured the nay on the BAFTA-nominated Assassin’s Creed Mirage soundtrack, and premiered his own concerto for the instrument, A Wildscape, at Southwark Cathedral. Ishaq also trained as a music therapist, which shapes how he builds a piece from the ground up—meant to hold and heal as much as to perform. His new work takes all of that and strips it back to where he started. JASAD (Arabic for body) was recorded live in his own Bethlehem studio with no band and no overdubs: just the nay and a frame drum strapped to his leg. Coltrane runs through it via Arabic maqam. Palestinian dabke footwork, learned while dancing professionally at school, translates directly onto the drum. Underneath it all is tashbib, the melodic-percussive Arabic woodwind tradition he grew up with. He refuses to call what he does a “revival”, to him, the tradition never went anywhere. On 24 October, he brings all of it to WOMEX in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, one stop on a tour running from Istanbul in September to the EFG London Jazz Festival in November. Below, he talks about breath, borders, and a living heritage, alongside an exclusive playlist of the tracks that shaped his sound. You play the nay while accompanying yourself on leg-percussion: one body producing melody and rhythm at once. For a first-time listener, how would you describe the sound and the setup? My sound is rooted in Palestinian and the broader Arabic musical tradition, while also drawing from Global Jazz and cross-cultural musical dialogue. I play the Nay flute and a leg-mounted frame drum at the same time. I sometimes describe what I do as similar to what an electronic music producer does, except my only playground is the Nay and the frame drum. I use them to build a live, layered and immersive sound, combining melodies, rhythms and acoustic effects in real time. I describe the frame drum as a natural extension of how I play the Nay, which involves a lot of percussive tonguing and playing with and around the rhythm. I also grew up dancing Palestinian Dabke professionally at school, which involves rhythmic stomping and movement. I translate some of the rhythmic footwork of Dabke onto the leg-mounted frame drum. It’s my own way of connecting movement to music. You were largely self-taught before Berklee, drawn to a reed flute dating back thousands of years. Was there a turning point that told you this instrument, and this path, were yours? The sound of the Nay was the turning point. I am largely self-taught on the Nay, but I started playing the euphonium at the Edward Said National Conservatory of Music in Palestine at the age of 12. When I was 16, my uncle had recently got some reed cane from Jericho and asked my older brother to make some holes in it so he could play. My brother made that flute, and my uncle never saw it again! This is how it started and I became obsessed with its sound. The other turning point was listening to Dhafer Youssef play live. His powerful presence and exploration of the voice touched me on a deep level, and I wanted to explore the Nay in a similar way. Your nay grows out of a shepherd’s music: you’ve revived the Palestinian tashbib. The Canaries have their own pastoral inheritance, including silbo gomero, the whistled language shepherds used to carry messages across the ravines of La Gomera. Is there anything in that shared open-air, herding root you’re curious to seek out while you’re in the islands? I wouldn’t say I revived Palestinian Tashbib. It was always there. The Nay has a long history across many cultures and countries, and similar reed flutes have taken many different forms and roles. I’m not sure the Nay grew only from shepherds’ music. I can definitely imagine that they started from that human desire to resonate with the natural beauty around us, open spaces, rivers and mountains. It’s fascinating how we developed such technologies through sound and our connection to the land. As you mentioned, silbo gomero is a beautiful example of this. In a similar way, Palestinian Tashbib is a melodic-percussive way of playing traditional woodwind instruments that goes by different names in Arab countries. In Palestine, we call it Tashbib, which literally means “to become young,” and it’s full of joy, rhythm and earthiness. Musically, it leaves space for improvisation and percussive interplay with and around the rhythms of traditional Palestinian songs and Dabke dance stomps. Essentially, to me, the rhythmic energy of Tashbib and the Dabke stomps are a way of showing dignity and our connection to the land and its soil. You bring the tashbib and jazz together on the nay. In a WOMEX line-up full of the world’s traditions, what makes yours stand out, and what do you hope people take from your showcase? I was particularly drawn to combining Tashbib and jazz because they both share an improvisational spirit connected with identity, as well as the rhythmic interplay of playing in and around the beat. But my album is not only about bringing Tashbib and jazz together. It’s about creating an immersive experience with the Nay that honours its roots and expansive musical potential, while also offering a grounding and healing space after the madness humanity has experienced in the past years. What stands out musically is that I create a complete world of musical expressions and sounds on the spot, using only the Nay and a leg-mounted frame drum. From that place, I combine Tashbib and Global Jazz influences with rich Arabic maqam modalities, Dabke and other rhythms, together with my original acoustic nay effects that have taken years to develop. All of these elements come together to create a singular musical language. The nay responds only to breath and intention: it’s an intimate instrument. How does playing to an attentive, close-listening delegate and music professional audience shape the way you perform? It will be an honour to share my music with music professionals from around the world. The very first thing the audience hears is how I feel in that moment, rather than a planned musical sentence. I shape my repertoire, improvisations, and textures according to how I feel at the start of the show and throughout the performance. For example, playing in a cathedral is very different from playing in a seated concert hall or to a standing audience. I enjoy resonating with the type of venue, atmosphere, and, most importantly, the audience, who mostly shape the musical journey. Playing for delegates and music professionals is the same. In the end, I want to create an immersive sonic journey that honours the sound of the Nay. You’re also a trained music therapist. Has that shaped how you think about what music is for, beyond the stage? Being trained as a music therapist has set the foundation for how I create music, helping me create work that is both musically and culturally rich, while carrying a sense of healing and grounding. Beyond WOMEX, what lies ahead: the JASAD project, new recordings, the concerto and orchestral directions you’ve been exploring? JASAD is currently set for an international tour, including the London Jazz Festival on November 14th, Melbourne Jazz Festival on October 18th, Arter in Istanbul on September 13th, and many other dates this autumn. Beyond this, I am working to expand my musical concerto A Wildscape, which premiered at Southwark Cathedral two years ago, while also working on a new album for jazz quartet.  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VT4Tbz0gm3A   On 24 October in Las Palmas, Faris Ishaq carries the memory of a homemade Jericho flute straight to the WOMEX stage, weaving Palestinian tashbib and global jazz into a singular live performance   PLAYLIST: FARIS ISHAQ X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   Cover Photo ©: Fadi Dahabreh The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Faris Ishaq appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 法里斯·伊沙克从伯利恒出发，在家中拾起一根来自杰里科的芦苇管，从此与奈伊笛结缘。他先在爱德华·萨伊德国家音乐学院学习上低音号，后凭全额奖学金进入伯克利全球爵士项目，将阿拉伯木卡姆体系植入爵士和声结构并获评顶尖学生。专辑《JASAD》（阿拉伯语意为"身体"）回到原点：在他自己的伯利恒工作室现场录制，仅用奈伊笛与绑在腿上的框鼓，无乐队、无叠录，一人同时承担旋律与节奏。作品中，约翰·柯川的爵士乐句经由阿拉伯木卡姆重塑，巴勒斯坦达布凯舞步直接转化为鼓点语言，底层流淌着他从小浸润的塔什比卜吹打传统。他为《刺客信条：幻景》原声带录制奈伊笛声部，并在伦敦南华克大教堂首演了自己的协奏曲《A Wildscape》，其音乐治疗师训练也渗透进创作逻辑中，使作品兼具疗愈与演出功能。

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦荷兰低音提琴手Arjen Gorter的个人专辑，他在欧洲先锋爵士界资历深厚，曾长期担任Willem Breuker Kollektief乐团的贝斯基石。专辑意在展现他脱离Breuker框架后的独立艺术身份。乐评追溯了他从阿姆斯特丹街头手风琴、尤克里里起步，最终走上低音提琴道路的曲折经历，以及1966年与Breuker首次合作并录制首张专辑的历程。文中涉及Gunter Hampel等欧洲自由爵士圈的合作录音，呈现了1960年代欧洲即兴音乐场景的横截面。作为Point of Departure刊发的深度乐评，文章兼具历史叙事与音乐分析，为理解欧洲先锋爵士低音提琴传统提供了珍贵视角。

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.
items.label: ezz-thetics 1070
items._genre: free improvisation / avant-garde jazz / contemporary composition
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由鼓手Gerry Hemingway领衔的国际乐队现场录音专辑，成员来自德国、爱尔兰、瑞士等地，乐器配置涵盖萨克斯、钢琴和贝斯。专辑延续了Hemingway在Anthony Braxton四重奏时期积累的创作语汇，以约36分钟的长曲为核心，穿插短小的钢琴二重奏即兴段落。长篇作品采用结构化的曲式框架，中间穿插自由即兴，叙事感强但偶有松散。演奏者将回收木料作为打击发声物融入演出，体现就地取材的实验精神。Hemingway的鼓风松弛自由，与钢琴手Izumi Kimura的预备钢琴音色高度契合，两人二重奏展现出极佳的呼吸感和音色互通。整体气质介于学院派自由爵士与当代作曲之间，适合偏好实验性现场即兴与文本化结构的听众。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德籍肯尼亚打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的双人组合Odd Okoddo，与83岁的肯尼亚传统歌手Ogoya Nengo首次三方合作。Nengo的加入带来了肯尼亚东部dodo传统歌唱的深厚底蕴，她与Ratengo在现场往来传递地域音乐记忆，而Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手鼓及套鼓则为人声提供弹性节奏支撑。《Bara》以重复打击模式开场，合成复节奏层层叠加，最终与两道人声自然融合；《Sarah》则通过Ratengo主唱与Kacirek试探性打击乐的配合，配合尖锐失真在声乐高潮处穿插出现。整张专辑展现了非洲传统与现代电子手段的对话，传统根源获得前卫表达，创新手段又呈现出千年古老质感，将跨文化合作推入更深层的融合领域。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Dorothy Moskowitz与意大利作曲家Paladino及诗人Ferrari合作，延续其六十年代实验乐队United States of America的脉络。十一首曲目以钢琴为核心，叠加弦乐、木管与合成器织体，形成非线性的音乐叙事，刻意摆脱西方和声运动的惯常逻辑。歌词层面延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统，《Charlottesville》直指极右翼政治话语，《Pale Wanderer》剖析威权主义所需的共谋结构，同时穿插对死亡与宇宙位置的哲思。Moskowitz的演唱以方法派演员般的权威感驾驭非对位旋律线，使每个词语的意义高于音乐本身的展开逻辑。整体制作模糊了歌曲与器乐曲的边界，是一张将政治反思、前卫作曲与诗歌文本熔于一炉的作品。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴厅完成了两小时无脚本的独奏即兴录音，作为专辑《Sendas》的基础素材。后期制作中稀疏地加入了人声采样、打击乐、循环片段、田野录音与拾得音效，形成多层纹理。Sosa 自述拒绝风格归类，融合爵士、拉丁、古典、电子等多重影响，强调'第一遍录制'作为灵魂的自然发声与'少即是多'的美学原则。专辑诞生于疫情期间个人生活变故与米兰演出取消的偶然交汇，地点本身具有深厚古典音乐传统背景。作品延续了他对冥想性、不断进化艺术创作的追求，将即兴钢琴置于田野录音与声音拼贴的语境中，呈现出融合传统与即兴精神的独奏钢琴新形态。

items.body: Archie Forde hails a compilation of young Icelandic electronic music makers, austere experimentalists and noisemongers, which rails against gentrification and foreclosed futures alike safn by plata It’s October 2025, and Icelandic noise music collective Spider Network are crammed into a Reykjavik beer garden, working late into the night. Spools of vermillion thread cling to the space’s tarp roof; one member laboriously unwraps tinfoil and plasters it across plastic windows and walls; a ritual doll is suspended from the ceiling.   This haunting decor is being assembled for Falconfest, a noise show held in Reykjavik venue Lemmy in collaboration with No Borders, a charity dedicated to providing mutual aid to refugees. Spider Network, who organised the gig, have homed in on harsh noise as a way to fight the closures of spaces... The post Compilation of the Week: Plata’s Safn appeared first on The Quietus.
items._genre: experimental electronic / harsh noise / Icelandic underground
items._cn_summary: 这张冰岛合辑汇集了当地年轻电子音乐创作者、严肃实验音乐人和噪音乐手，背景设定在2025年10月雷克雅未克的Spider Network噪音音乐场景。组织者以极端噪音为表达手段，反抗城市士绅化和音乐空间的关闭。合辑与No Borders难民慈善机构合作举办Falconfest演出，演出现场布满红色线轴、锡箔和仪式感玩偶等装置，营造出仪式化的噪音场域。整张合辑将冰岛地下电子生态与激进社会议题结合，声音取向偏向粗糙、极端、非旋律化，带有鲜明的反建制色彩，适合对极端实验声响和北欧地下场景感兴趣的听众。

items.body: John X Belmonte’s Golden Lore understands a basic truth about goth clubs, doomed romance, and every terrible decision made after midnight: grandeur works best when there is something embarrassing hiding underneath it. The song moves with the confidence of a man walking into a ruined cathedral wearing sunglasses, fully aware that vanity and remorse have been sharing the same coat for years. Its synth bass keeps the floor moving with a steady, narcotic insistence, while Belmonte’s voice sits low in the mix, deep and controlled, as though he is delivering private evidence to a room that has already reached its verdict. The pitch-shifted echo curling around the vocal gives Belmonte’s delivery a doubled quality, part confession and part apparition, suggesting memory as a badly behaved accomplice rather than some sacred archive. Golden Lore keeps circling myth, beauty, regret, and self-invention, those old poisons that people pour into prettier bottles whenever reality starts looking cheap. The lyrics seem fascinated by how easily memory turns vanity into legend, and how legend eventually gets mistaken for truth. Golden Lore belongs to that hour when the dance floor becomes less a public space than a private reckoning set to a bassline. Belmonte gives the song enough romantic scale to make regret feel almost luxurious, letting memory dress its worst decisions in expensive clothes. By the final chorus, desire, vanity, and remorse have become impossible to separate, and the song leaves them circling one another beneath the club lights until closing time. As a dance track, Golden Lore has excellent instincts. The rhythm remains disciplined, the bassline stays heavy, and every element serves the forward motion. Nothing gets cluttered for the sake of drama. Then the chorus opens up, and this is where the song earns its black clothes. The melody is gorgeous without becoming sugary, large without losing its bruised center. There is a real sense of release in the refrain, the kind that makes a crowded room briefly feel communal even when everyone inside it is busy maintaining their own private disaster. You can hear why fans of Cold Cave, Drab Majesty, Then Comes Silence, and the Sisters of Mercy might find an immediate point of entry, though Belmonte keeps enough restraint in the arrangement to avoid drowning the song in borrowed gestures. The video takes a similarly direct route. Belmonte performs against images of a mysterious figure moving through a dark landscape with a giant ankh, the superimposition giving the clip the look of damaged film discovered in somebody’s locked drawer. The imagery is simple, but it suits the song’s obsession with memory, myth, and the ghostly versions of ourselves we keep polishing. Watch the video for Golden Lore below: Based in New York City, John X Belmonte is an independent darkwave and post-punk artist drawn to the romantic and cinematic possibilities of gothic music. His work pairs brooding atmosphere with rhythmic urgency, giving beauty and emotional intensity equal room within its electronic arrangements. Released September 18, 2026, Golden Lore brings that sensibility to its examination of myth, memory, and remorse. Listen to Golden Lore on Spotify here. Follow John X. items.body: Seduction gets complicated when one person knows the future, and the other is still getting accustomed to being human. Geneva Jacuzzi takes that imbalance to an entertaining extreme on Nu2U, a song she described in a 2024 interview with The FADER as an encounter between a primordial being and a caveman. Sex comes with a preview of the centuries ahead, including the suffering humanity has yet to invent for itself. Some lovers bring emotional baggage; this one brings the entire future of civilization. The Los Angeles musician and multimedia artist now gives that peculiar proposition a theatrical setting in the video for Nu2U, taken from her third album, Triple Fire, released on Dais Records in August 2024. Produced by Jacuzzi with co-production from Josh da Costa, the track supplies an appropriately crooked dance floor for an encounter across the ages. Nu2U bubbles and clangs with eerie, clamorous synths and foot-stomping percussion, making a persuasive case for synth music for cavemen. The occasional, emphatic keyboard stabs have an unmistakably prehistoric character, placing the track in the same mischievous tribe as Toto Coelo’s “I Eat Cannibals,” but if they ate edibles instead of flesh. Beneath that primal stomp, an intricate, melodic bassline curls through the arrangement, deepening the groove and giving its heavy steps a supple, sensual movement. Jacuzzi’s cool delivery, evocative of Erotica-era Madonna, presides over the gathering with a shamanic poise, her voice suggesting secret knowledge passed between bodies. The whole thing acquires a ritualistic pull, as though the discovery of electricity has given an ancient fertility dance some intriguing new possibilities. Directed and edited by Jacuzzi, with cinematography and art direction by Shannon Cornett, the video places its performers inside a set that recreates a work by artist Steven Arnold. Costumes are credited to Stacy Ellen Rich and Jacuzzi, with lighting by Tom Nixon and Fred Joseph. The official video credits make clear how many hands went into this compact, extravagantly strange production. Jacuzzi presides over a miniature theatre of cutout flames, suspended shapes, spirals, and stars, wearing an enormous geometric headdress above a pale costume punctuated with black circles. Her painted face and deliberate gestures suggest a celestial hostess who has been repeating this demonstration for several thousand years. Around her, figures pose in sculpted torso pieces, metallic-looking body paint, and elaborate accessories, turning the human form into another decorative element in the set. Deep blue lighting gives way to hot pink, red, and green, while stark monochrome close-ups interrupt the wider tableaux. Faces fill the frame; arms lift and bend; a crescent becomes a frame within the frame. The visibly handmade scenery lends the spectacle the intimacy of a toy theatre, even when its inhabitants look capable of rearranging the cosmos. There is a lovely absurdity to the scale of it all: the future of humanity appears to be under discussion in a cabaret small enough to pack into a van. Watch the video for “Nu2U” below: That meeting of pop music, costume, and performance has long been central to Jacuzzi’s work. Following Lamaze and Technophelia, Triple Fire brought her songs into sharper focus while preserving their appetite for strange characters and exaggerated situations. With Nu2U, another of those characters gets a stage, a formidable hat, and a captive audience. Triple Fire is available through Dais Records and Bandcamp. Triple Fire by Geneva Jacuzzi Geneva Jacuzzi is set to perform at The Chapel in San Francisco on September 19, 2026. She will be joined by EX-HEIR, Diesel Dudes, and Nick Moss, who will also DJ. Doors open at 8 p.m., and the all-ages show starts at 9 p.m. Tickets are available here. items.body: alarm!systemen self-titled Antibody Belgian newcomer alarm!systemen’s debut LP has a range of sounds and approaches which often belies a lack of direction or aesthetic, but that’s definitely not the case here. At large, the ten tracks on offer draw from long histories of coldwave and dream pop, but eschew slavish adherence to lo-fi nostalgia for its own sake. The classic Slowdive-isms of “Goes Again” are offset by clean, if minimal modern programming, and later on album closer “Void” serves as a reminder of how that act and other shoegaze giants found new life lifting from ambient electronics at large. On the more direct side, “Kapot” juxtaposes bricked-out synthpop drum programming with excellently reverbed guitar, and the dead simple but wonderfully executed dream pop nod of “BURN” shows just how far some wistful melodies and airy production can take you when they’re done with a measure of taste and restraint. Written over the course of five years, it’s perhaps not surprising that there’s this much variety here, but alarm!systemen’s real forte is in pulling it all off well enough to refresh familiar styles and serve as an example of how younger acts drawn to these classic sounds can rework and rethink them in their own manner. alarm!systemen by alarm!systemen Zataar First Crush CRVSH While based in France, the material released by producer Zataar draws from both her Morrocan and Belgian heritage. From the latter, you funky rhythmic electronics that hearken back to the New Beat era with a healthy dose of classic body music, where the former comes through in the melodies and instrumentation that reference North African folk music. Cuts like “Ali Sawtek” lean into the blend especially well, finding a swinging groove in the bass and drum programming, while Zataar’s vocals and the track’s melody are kept low and swirling in the mix, with big string stabs cutting through the thick reverb. As a contrast, “In the Lights You Call My Name” injects polyrhythmic complexity into the drum track, its belchy resonant bassline flowing beneath rich waves of plucks and pads. The cleverness in the arrangements really comes through on “Moments in Love”, which manages transitions between deep house styled rhythm programming and sections of Chaabi folk melodies, before combining them smoothly into a hypnotic whole. Far from a gimmick, it’s a fully realized approach that recognizes the commonality and contrasts inherent in blending multiple styles and genres, and then reconciles them handily. items.body: Review by tmay102436 — I have been following Compassionizer for many years now, and have always been amazed with their music.This new outing� - "The Faithful of the Land" is a further extension of their consistent growth as both musicians and composers, with this being not as much a change in direction, but taking an exciting continuation / exploration of their style. The mixture of instrumentation is beautifully executed and the vocal "shadows" during the music, enhances the texture and atmosphere in an eerie, enjoyable way.Especially notable is the sensitive use of synth, as you hardly know it's there, but then it appears beautifully. Along with this is the basic "guitar / bass / drums" - making it Rock Music, with orchestration melding into the presentation seamlessly. 21st Century Music at its best!BRAVO! 5 starts!
items._cn_summary: 这是一张延续乐队既有风格的专辑，没有大幅转向，而是在原有基础上做进一步的探索与拓展。编曲中器乐层次丰富，合成器以细腻的方式嵌入，几乎不被察觉却又在关键时刻浮现，与吉他、贝斯、鼓的基础摇滚框架形成呼应。管弦乐编排无缝融入整体，增添深度与色彩。人声以类似"阴影"的形式穿插于器乐段落，营造出怪诞却迷人的氛围与质感。整体呈现出一种21世纪音乐的面貌，在前卫摇滚的传统结构内引入实验性的音色处理与情绪铺陈。评论者作为长期听众，肯定了这支乐队多年来的稳定成长轨迹。

items.body: “Caminando Por La Playa” means walking along the beach, yet Aldo Zolev wrote it about a happy day marching through Bogotá, a city more than 2,600 metres up in the Andes and hundreds of kilometres from the sea. The percussion sets a brisk marching step through the instrumental, with Sandro Londoño on cymbals. Sandra Duque plays the melody on bassoon over Zolev’s double bass. Zolev describes the piece as energetic and lively, built on a memory of Colombian rhythms, and says the walk stands for a way through life, urging his friends to walk “por la vida hoy y siempre“, through life today and always, and to be happy. Zolev comes from Pamplona, a small Andean city in north-eastern Colombia near the Venezuelan border, where his grandfather, a professional double bassist, started him on the instrument. He moved to Bogotá to study double bass at the conservatory of the Universidad Nacional de Colombia and took jazz and harmony lessons with saxophonist Antonio Arnedo. He formed the world-jazz group Dos Aguas and later played in Bereket, an ensemble devoted to Turkish and Middle Eastern music. In 2007 he set up EnnO, the independent Bogotá label and studio that has since produced 25 albums and runs its own world music festival. Three years later he launched UVA Sexteto, bringing the oud in alongside his double bass. He has also recorded with MARIAZÚ, whose album Eau de Vie – Agua Ardiente was cut outdoors in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, with birdsong and running water around acoustic instruments and indigenous percussion. In 2025 Zolev relaunched Sensaciones Bajo La Lluvia, the album that carries “Caminando Por La Playa”, and he has just come back from a summer tour of Europe. items._cn_summary: 这是波哥大低音提琴手 Aldo Zolev 作品《Caminando Por La Playa》的乐评。曲名意为「沿海滩漫步」，但创作灵感来自安第斯山脉城市波哥大的一次欢乐行军，与海洋无关。配乐由 Sandro Londoño 负责钹声，奠定明快的行进节奏；Sandra Duque 用巴松演奏旋律，叠于 Zolev 的低音提琴之上。Zolev 来自哥伦比亚北部安第斯小城潘普洛纳，其祖父是职业低音提琴手，他先后在波哥大国立大学音乐学院学习低音提琴，跟随萨克斯演奏家 Antonio Arnedo 学习爵士与和声。他组建过世界爵士乐团 Dos Aguas，参与过土耳其与中东音乐合奏 Bereket，2007 年创立独立厂牌 EnnO 并运营世界音乐节，2010 年成立将欧乌德琴与低音提琴并置的 UVA Sexteto。他还与 MARIAZÚ 合作，在圣玛尔塔雪山户外录制专辑，捕捉鸟鸣与流水声与原住民打击乐器的交织。2025 年他重新发行收录此曲的专辑《Sensaciones Bajo La Lluvia》，近期完成欧洲巡演。

items.body: Laho is a Finnish project that originated in 2006. After releasing a few records during its early years, the project went quiet for a long time before being reactivated a few years ago. “Death Machines”—which feels more like a seven-track mini-album—was inspired by today’s dystopian world, as well as by self-reflection and other dark themes. The music is indeed quite dark, but that is not the whole story. This record reveals two sides: on the one hand, a powerful production featuring menacing yet brilliant basslines topped with razor-sharp sequences; on the other, a completely different style with a Cinematic feel, including one entirely instrumental track. Personally, I prefer Laho’s harder side, which occasionally reminds me of early Combichrist, albeit with a certain polished touch. This is also evident in the vocal production, which is powerful yet has something of a ‘Power-Pop’ quality. It comes as no surprise, then, that the album concludes with a remarkable cover of Depeche Mode‘s “Behind the Wheel,” delivered in a dark and intense style. I think it’s a great track, by the way. Laho seems to be a sort of Janus—a two-faced project, with its powerful side completely winning me over. (Rating:7½). Listen to “The Great Collapse”: The Great Collapse by Laho About Laho Laho is a Finnish dark electronic project led by musician and recording engineer Konsta Vehkala, who is based in Jyväskylä and is responsible for all composition, programming and production. The project is an outlet for solo works by Vehkala and blends industrial, EBM, futurepop and darkwave. The project began in 2006 under the name Lahonnut Konkelo as a series of electronic and industrial experiments. The name was shortened to Laho shortly afterwards. The first EP, “The Other Side”, appeared in 2007 as an independently issued CDr, combining instrumental industrial metal with a slightly experimental edge. It was later re-released by Italian netlabel Ekleipsi, which also issued the first full-length album “Escape from the Dying Star” in 2009. “Escape from the Dying Star” was recorded between 2007 and 2008 at the Cable_Hell studio and released digitally in April 2009, offering a mix of electro-industrial, cybernetic synth work and distorted guitar. The album held ten tracks including “Program”, “Dead End” and a remix by Technomancer. Later in 2009 Laho issued “The World in Flames” as a standalone digital release, followed by the single “Mechanigod” in 2011 and a one-off digital track “Walking in the Air (1984 mix)” in December 2021. After these early EP and album releases, the project entered a 13-year hiatus as Vehkala focused on other bands and production work. Writing for Laho resumed in 2024, leading to a new series of songs, this time including vocals. Parallel to Laho, Vehkala maintains an active role in the Finnish metal scene. He plays drums for the melodic metal band Psychework and has performed and recorded with groups including Gian, Vipermilk and Lojohh, as well as contributing recording, mixing and mastering work to a wide range of Finnish underground acts. “Death Machines” is Laho’s first release since writing resumed in 2024, and its first EP built around vocals throughout.
items._cn_summary: 芬兰黑暗电子项目Laho由Konsta Vehkala独自操刀，融合工业、EBM、futurepop与暗潮元素。这张数字EP呈现两面性：一面以强劲制作、凶狠贝斯线与锋利音序构成压迫感，嗓音偏Power-Pop的明亮质感与之形成张力；另一面转向电影化的氛围铺陈，包含一首纯器乐曲目。专辑主题围绕当代反乌托邦与自我反思展开，以Depeche Mode经典翻唱收尾，在保留原作骨架的同时注入黑暗工业的强度。整体制作精致且具有个人辨识度，硬朗一面尤为突出，独立厂牌发行也保持了地下气质。

items.body: There’s a kind of idiotic joy in doing the thing you know might end with blood on your shirt, a phone call at 3 a.m., or somebody asking what in God’s name you were thinking. Maybe that’s the point. Responsibility has its virtues, sure, but it has lousy rhythm. Danger gives stupidity a backbeat. You leap, you laugh, you watch the floor come up fast, and afterward you stand there amid the wreckage with a shrug that says maybe it was worth it, maybe it wasn’t, and maybe asking the question ruins half the fun anyway. Consequences are tomorrow’s problem. Bad decisions have always needed better music. Nobody ever ruined their life because the bassline was too sensible, and Copenhagen-born artist In Atlas seems to understand that civilization periodically requires somebody to hand the evening over to the little red bastard sitting on your shoulder. Tears, Poison, Desire, the first single from her forthcoming Hyperreal LP, out November 5 through Detriti Records, concerns that exquisite stretch of time when every warning sign has become decorative. You can hear Lizzy Mercier Descloux in its crooked dance-floor instincts, Lene Lovich and Suburban Lawns in its elastic theatricality, and a buzzing chaos reminiscent of Suicide, Tuxedomoon, and DAF lurking around the song’s machinery. The beat keeps things moving while the voice plays around its edges, cool one second, knowingly absurd the next. Dark disco becomes less a genre designation than an excuse to behave badly under flattering dancefloor lights. And why shouldn’t it? Half the supposed wisdom of adulthood consists of learning exactly which pleasures you’re expected to decline, usually because somebody older already enjoyed them first and left you the cleanup bill. “Let’s say its about coming apart in the desire for some sort of liberation, or maybe its about having fun, or maybe about having a kind of fun you don’t really want to have, being spurred on by that little red guy on your shoulder,” says the artist. “Playing with fire, then playing with the embers, then playing with gasoline.” Now that is a philosophy worth dancing to. The important word may be “gasoline,” because fire is charming enough when it belongs to candles and cigarettes; eventually somebody discovers what happens when you pour something stupid onto it. Desire works similarly. So does freedom. Push either far enough and you may find yourself staring at the remains the next morning, unable to decide whether you have learned anything or merely acquired a better story. Listen to Tears, Poison, Desire below, or via streaming here. That ambivalence runs through the upcoming Hyperreal, an album concerned with escapism and private worlds meeting an uncooperative reality. In Atlas, also one half of Greek/Danish duo V.V.I.A. alongside Venus Volcanism, seems drawn to the ecstatic and ridiculous point where pleasure starts growing teeth. Perhaps consequences deserve respect. They are very punctual. But while Tears, Poison, Desire is blaring, tomorrow can stand outside and knock. Follow In Atlas: Instagram Spotify Soundcloud The post Danish Post-Punk Artist In Atlas Gives the Devil on Her Shoulder a Say in “Tears, Poison, Desire” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
